Nationwide Protests Disrupt Mexican Economy; Petroleos Mexicanos Operations Hampered

MEXICO CITY, June 14 — Widespread protests and road blockades have paralyzed key transport corridors across Mexico for a fourth consecutive day, disrupting supply chains and forcing several major companies, including Petroleos Mexicanos, to curtail operations.

The unrest, sparked by public anger over proposed constitutional reforms affecting regional autonomy and resource management, has led to demonstrations in at least 18 states. Truck convoys and access roads to major ports are blocked, with the central industrial belt around Querétaro and the Gulf of Mexico oil hub particularly affected.

Petroleos Mexicanos reported delays in crude shipments from the Dos Bocas terminal, and said some refinery operations were “temporarily scaled back” due to shortages of critical supplies. “We are prioritizing safety and focusing on maintaining essential services,” a company spokesperson said. “We urge all parties to seek a peaceful resolution.”

The National Chamber of Commerce said early estimates suggest nationwide economic losses could top $850 million since the protests began, as factories struggle with interrupted deliveries and exporters miss overseas deadlines.

Small businesses have been hit as well, with many closing temporarily due to supply disruptions and security concerns. “We haven’t received flour in three days, and our bakery is down to its last bags,” said Ana Gómez, a shop owner in Puebla.

President Andrés Manuel López Obrador appealed for calm in a televised address, stating the government is “committed to dialogue.” Meanwhile, the Mexican Confederation of Workers called on the administration to “listen to citizens’ demands and restore order.”

With talks between protest leaders and officials ongoing, analysts warn that prolonged unrest could further dent economic growth and investor confidence.
